settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The algorithm.none path requires parts.length == 2 (lines 69, 119); a 3-part signed token with alg=none will instead reach the verifier loop and, with a verifier present, fail canVerify for none (HMACVerifier/RSAVerifier only return true for their own algorithms), so a normal signed flow is not bypassed.
In the Verifier... overload the none branch requires verifiers.length == 0, so a caller that always passes at least one verifier is protected there.
The unsecured path is explicitly documented as intentional ('Be particular about decoding an unsecured JWT').
candidates.description: In JWTDecoder, both decode overloads short-circuit to returning the payload when header.algorithm == Algorithm.none, the token has exactly two parts, and either no varargs verifiers (line 69) or an empty verifier map (line 119) are present. The unsecured branch deserializes parts[1] and returns it as a JWT. Because the unsecured check is placed BEFORE the verifier lookup/verification logic (decode(encodedJWT, header, parts, verifier) at lines 81/132), the algorithm reported in the attacker-controlled header controls whether signature verification runs at all. A token of the form base64({"alg":"none"}).base64(payload). (note the trailing dot, which is what makes getParts() accept a 2-element array per lines 174-182) is returned unverified. The guard only blocks the unsecured path when a verifier map/array is non-empty AND the length/format conditions differ; with the RSA/HMAC decode(encodedJWT, Verifier...) overloads the none branch is only reachable when verifiers.length == 0, but with the map overload decode(String, Map) an empty map lets an alg=none token through without verification. The deeper design issue is that the caller's intent to require verification (a verifier was provided) does not override the token's self-declared alg=none.
missing_evidence: No test in the repo exercises an alg=none token against decode(...) to confirm the bypass and the exact part-length/trailing-dot requirement.
No application call sites are present in this repo, so real-world reachability with an empty map (line 119) or zero varargs (line 69) is unconfirmed.
The library does not document an explicit 'reject none' policy or configuration flag; absence of such a flag could not be confirmed as a vulnerability vs. a caller responsibility.
preconditions: Application decodes untrusted JWTs using JWTDecoder.decode(String, Map<String,Verifier>) with an empty or attacker-influenceable verifier map, or otherwise relies on the decoder to reject unsigned tokens.
Token is a 2-part dot-separated string with header alg=none and a trailing dot.
No external layer already rejects alg=none tokens or strips the trailing-dot form.
candidates.title: Unsigned JWT (alg=none) accepted even when verifiers are supplied

counter_evidence: canVerify is purely algorithm-based by design; with a single verifier the selection is unambiguous.
The map overload decode(String, Map) plus keyFunction explicitly supports kid-based selection, suggesting multi-key selection is expected to go through that API.
The verifier==null case correctly throws MissingVerifierException instead of skipping verification.
candidates.description: In decode(String, Verifier...) the loop at lines 74-79 iterates all verifiers and, for each one that reports canVerify(header.algorithm) == true, assigns verifier = v. Because canVerify only checks the header-declared algorithm (HMACVerifier.canVerify returns true for HS256/384/512; RSAVerifier for RS256/384/512), multiple verifiers may accept and the LAST match wins, with `verifier` left null if none match. When parts.length == 3 and verifier == null the code throws MissingVerifierException (lines 149-151), which is correct. However there is no binding between the token's `kid`/`x5t` header values and a specific key in this overload (the map overload handles kid via keyFunction). A caller who passes several public keys/secrets to the varargs overload intending 'this token must be signed by key K' can have verification performed against any verifier that merely advertises support for the header algorithm, not necessarily the intended key. This is a key-selection trust issue rather than a direct signature bypass.
missing_evidence: No documentation or test showing intended semantics for multiple same-algorithm verifiers in the varargs overload.
No evidence any caller passes multiple same-algorithm verifiers; behavior may be harmless in practice.
preconditions: Caller uses decode(String, Verifier...) with multiple verifiers covering the same algorithm family.
Caller expects the verifier choice to be constrained by key identifier (kid/x5t) rather than only by algorithm.
candidates.title: Signature verification result stored but algorithm not re-bound to verifier in varargs decode loop

counter_evidence: InvalidJWTException is thrown for the clearly malformed 3-or-2-part cases, indicating some input validation is intentional.
base64Decode wraps IllegalArgumentException into InvalidJWTException (lines 135-141), showing defensiveness elsewhere.
An uncaught RuntimeException on malformed input typically results in a failed request, not a privilege gain.
candidates.description: getParts(String) splits on '.' and accepts the result when parts.length == 3 or (length == 2 && endsWith('.')). decode then unconditionally indexes parts[0] (line 66/117) and parts[1] (line 70/120, 159) and computes encodedJWT.lastIndexOf('.') (line 144). For a 2-part value that does NOT end with a dot, or for degenerate inputs, InvalidJWTException is thrown (acceptable), but inputs such as a single '.' or a string that splits into 2 parts without the trailing-dot handling can still drive indexing assumptions. More concretely, in the unsecured branch parts[1] is used without a length check beyond the header check; the header itself is parsed from parts[0] before any validation that parts[0] is non-empty. Additionally RSAUtils.getKeyBytes (line 192-197) calls key.indexOf(prefix)/indexOf(suffix) and then substring on the result without verifying the indices are != -1, so a key string that contains the prefix but not the suffix (or vice versa) throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException rather than a controlled error. These are robustness/DoS-style issues on malformed input rather than authentication bypass.
missing_evidence: No test demonstrates the index-out-of-bounds paths for getParts or getKeyBytes.
Unclear whether callers wrap decode() in exception handling that would neutralize DoS impact.
preconditions: Caller passes attacker-controlled or malformed JWT/key strings
No upstream validation or try/catch that maps these runtime exceptions to a safe response
candidates.title: Malformed JWT input can trigger unchecked NullPointerException / ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

counter_evidence: exp/nbf are enforced with exceptions (JWTExpiredException / JWTUnavailableForProcessingException), so time-based claims are not ignored.
Audience/issuer validation is commonly a caller responsibility and the fields are exposed for the caller to check; absence here is not necessarily a defect.
No leeway parameter may be intentional to keep the API simple.
candidates.description: JWT.isExpired (line 290-291) and isUnavailableForProcessing (line 300-301) compare against ZonedDateTime.now(ZoneOffset.UTC) with no leeway/clock-skew tolerance, and JWTDecoder.decode validates only exp and nbf. There is no audience (aud) or issuer (iss) validation in the decoder. If a deployment relies solely on decode() to enforce token validity, tokens may be accepted for a different intended audience/issuer, or rejected/accepted at the clock boundary in ways a caller may not expect. The audience and issuer fields are parsed but never validated anywhere in the decoder path.
missing_evidence: No application call sites in the repo to show whether aud/iss are validated by the caller after decode().
No documentation stating whether audience/issuer checks and clock skew are intentionally out of scope.
preconditions: Application relies on JWTDecoder to enforce that the token is intended for a specific audience/issuer.
Clock skew between issuer and verifier exists, or multiple issuers share a signing key.
candidates.title: Expiration/not-before validation uses strict no-skew comparison and no audience/issuer checks in decoder
